- Tampered digest: `localhost:5000/juice-shop@sha256:c64c687cbea9300178b30c95835354e34c4e4febc4badfe27102879de0483b5e`

### Original digest verification — PASSED

```json
[{"critical":{"identity":{"docker-reference":"localhost:5000/juice-shop@sha256:28870b9d2bec49e605d6ebbf4b22ed1ec1ca0a72347ef19217bbbb21ea44e3fe"},"image":{"docker-manifest-digest":"sha256:28870b9d2bec49e605d6ebbf4b22ed1ec1ca0a72347ef19217bbbb21ea44e3fe"},"type":"https://sigstore.dev/cosign/sign/v1"},"optional":null}]

### Tampered digest verification — FAILED correctly

Error: no signatures found
error during command execution: no signatures found
```

### Original digest sanity verification — PASSED again

```json
[{"critical":{"identity":{"docker-reference":"localhost:5000/juice-shop@sha256:28870b9d2bec49e605d6ebbf4b22ed1ec1ca0a72347ef19217bbbb21ea44e3fe"},"image":{"docker-manifest-digest":"sha256:28870b9d2bec49e605d6ebbf4b22ed1ec1ca0a72347ef19217bbbb21ea44e3fe"},"type":"https://sigstore.dev/cosign/sign/v1"},"optional":null}]
```

### Why digest binding matters

An OCI tag is a mutable pointer, while the digest is a cryptographic identifier for one
specific manifest and content graph. The Alpine image could be pushed under a convincing
Juice Shop tag, but it resolved to a different digest and therefore had no matching
signature. Signing a tag as a name without resolving and binding the immutable digest
would allow later tag movement to create false trust in different bytes.

### SLSA provenance attestation

- Builder ID: `https://github.com/inno-devops-labs/DevSecOps-Intro/labs/lab8`
- Build type: `https://slsa.dev/provenance/v0.2`

Verification output:

```json
{"payload":"","payloadType":"application/vnd.in-toto+json","signatures":[{"sig":"MEUCIQDDingWs1V2IblHAVs3xwGCrslVRMcH4jyXOAWa0mCUggIgL5wXykMCjrDqswRN4tQ1ZYdPDPbzRlC3kNnJL+LAQ3c="}]}
```

### What this gives an admission-time verifier

A signature establishes who authorized one immutable image digest, while the verified
SBOM and provenance attestations make machine-readable claims about its contents and
origin. At admission time, a policy engine can require both the signature and predicates
such as the expected builder or SBOM type. When a new vulnerability such as Log4Shell is
announced, the SBOM allows inventory queries without rebuilding or rescanning every
running image from scratch.

## Bonus: Blob Signing — Codecov 2021 Mitigation

### Blob signing

```text
Using payload from: labs/lab8/results/my-tool.tar.gz
Wrote bundle to file labs/lab8/results/my-tool.tar.gz.bundle
MEUCIQCbAlWMzkHTN0rZBRqvKWpFM6R3DqKEf1WiW2GVqlNmpwIgItBlL9bv7WkWLTnLNL9T4gs3yLX2POsb99rcjMVcSTQ=
```

### Original blob verification — PASSED

```text
WARNING: Skipping tlog verification is an insecure practice that lacks transparency and auditability verification for the blob.
Verified OK
```

### Tampered blob verification — FAILED correctly

```text
WARNING: Skipping tlog verification is an insecure practice that lacks transparency and auditability verification for the blob.
Error: failed to verify signature: could not verify message: invalid signature when validating ASN.1 encoded signature
error during command execution: failed to verify signature: could not verify message: invalid signature when validating ASN.1 encoded signature
```

### Why this mitigates the Codecov attack class

A consumer that downloads an installer should run `cosign verify-blob --key cosign.pub
--bundle my-tool.tar.gz.bundle my-tool.tar.gz` before executing it. Any attacker-modified
byte stream produces a different digest and fails verification, so the compromised
artifact is rejected before `bash` or another interpreter can execute it. This removes
the unauthenticated `curl | bash` trust assumption exploited in the Codecov incident.
